\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{[{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+1]\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\text{d}x & = \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+C & .\end{aligned}
$$

From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =x-\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ {cot}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(1-{cot}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4}))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(1-{csc}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2-{csc}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4}))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}2\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}{csc}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}+\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4}){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+0-1 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad  \cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Using the Secant-Tangent Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a $\tan^2{x}$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+\tan^2x =\sec^2x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
\tan^2 x =\sec^2 x -1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \tan^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \left(\sec^2 x -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\tan x -x+C.	
	}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Using the Cosecant-Cotangent Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+\cot^2x =\csc^2 x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\cot^2 x &=\csc^2 x -1.
}
$$

Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \left(5\cot^2 x -x^2\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \bigg(5\left(\csc^2 x -1 \right) -x^2\bigg) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\int \left(5\csc^2 x -5 -x^2\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=-5\cot x -5x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.	
	}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Trigonometric Expressions With Linear Arguments Using the Pythagorean Identities
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta$ with $\theta = 3x,$ we get 

$$
\eqalign{
		1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\
		\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1.
}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                &= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                 &= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\
				                                &= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\
                                                                 &= 	\dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C.
	}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
How can we calculate  $\displaystyle{\int} \left(3\sin^2 x + 3\cos^2 x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x?$

We can compute integrals like this using the Pythagorean trigonometric identity, 

$$
\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x=1.
$$

So, we evaluate our integral as follows: 

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \left(3\sin^2 x+  3\cos^2 x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x  &=  \int 3(\underbrace{\sin^2 x +\cos^2 x }_1 )\, \textrm{d}x\
				                                                                &=\int 3(1) \, \textrm{d}x\
				                                                                &=\int 3  \, \textrm{d}x\
				                                                                &=3x+C
}
$$

Let's look at some more examples.

tutorials.name: Calculating Integrals Using Related Identities
tutorials.problem:
The identities 

$$
1+\tan ^{2}x =\sec ^{2}x
$$

and

$$
1+\cot ^{2}x =\csc ^{2}x
$$

are also called Pythagorean trigonometric identities. They can be used to solve certain integrals involving the expressions 
$\tan^2 x$ or  $\csc^2 x.$ Let's see their application in action!
